title: The Sock Monster
paragraphs:
A monster lives in our kitchen.
It’s square and it’s shiny and white,
with one round eye made of glass
that watches us all day and night.

On Mondays, Dad feeds it our washing.
It gulps it all down with a slurp,
then it churns and it spins like a whirlwind
and finishes off with a burp.

But when Dad takes out all the washing
and sorts all the socks into pairs,
there’s always a sock that has vanished,
and Dad scratches his head and just stares.

“It’s the monster!” I tell him. “It’s greedy!
It swallows our socks for its tea!
It sucks them up just like spaghetti!”
But Dad only chuckles at me.

So one Monday, I hid by the fridge,
as quiet and still as a mouse,
to catch that sock-gobbling monster
before it could gobble the house.

Then a nose poked into the washing basket
and pulled out a sock, stripy blue.
It trotted away with its treasure.
I tiptoed behind it. Guess who?

It was our dog! In her bed in the hallway,
on a mountain of socks, she pretended to sleep.
So I crept back and patted the monster
and said sorry. It gave a soft beep.

questions.prompt:
Look at verses 1 and 2.
What is the ‘monster’ really? Tick **one**.

Look at verse 2.
The monster ‘spins like a whirlwind’.
What does this tell you about the monster? Tick **one**.
options: It is standing outside in a storm.
It spins round slowly and gently.
It blows cold air around the kitchen.

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 3.
There is always a sock that ‘has vanished’.
Which word is closest in meaning to **vanished**? Tick **one**.

Look at verse 3.
‘Dad scratches his head and just stares.’
How does Dad feel? Tick **one**.

Look at verse 4.
Find and copy **one** word that shows Dad thinks the speaker’s idea is funny.

Look at the whole poem.
Tick **one** box in each row to show whether each statement is **true** or **false**.
statements: The monster is square and shiny.
Dad feeds the monster every day.
The speaker hid by the fridge.
The monster has two glass eyes.

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 6.
Which sock was pulled out of the washing basket? Tick **one**.

Look at verse 6.
Why does this verse end with the question ‘Guess who?’ Tick **one**.
options: to show that Dad is asking the speaker a question
to show that the monster is talking to the speaker
to make the reader guess who took the sock before the next verse tells them
to show that the speaker has forgotten the dog’s name

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 7.
Where was the dog’s bed?

Look at verse 7.
Why does the speaker say sorry to the monster?
Explain, using evidence from the poem.
questions.model: The speaker had blamed the monster for the missing socks, saying ‘It swallows our socks for its tea!’ But then the speaker found the dog lying ‘on a mountain of socks’, so the speaker realised that the dog had been taking them and the monster had done nothing wrong.
points: Explains that the speaker had blamed the monster for eating the socks, with evidence, such as ‘It’s the monster!’ or ‘It swallows our socks for its tea!’
Explains that the dog had really taken the socks, so the monster was not to blame, with evidence, such as ‘on a mountain of socks’.

questions.prompt: Which is the best summary of the whole poem? Tick **one**.
options: A washing machine breaks down and floods the kitchen.
Dad buys new socks because all the old ones have holes in them.
A child blames the washing machine for eating socks, but finds out that the dog has been taking them.
A dog gets lost in the house while looking for its bed.
